groups.high: Margin trading uses borrowed funds or leveraged exposure to control a position larger than the trader's own equity. At 10x initial leverage, $1,000 of equity supports a $10,000 position. In a simplified long-position example, a 10% fall in the asset produces a $1,000 loss, exhausting the initial equity before interest and fees. A 1% move initially changes that equity by roughly 10%, in either direction. This arithmetic assumes unchanged exposure and does not specify the broker's liquidation price. Initial margin differs from maintenance margin, the minimum equity required to keep a position open. A margin call or forced sale may occur before equity reaches zero. Rapid price gaps, fees and financing costs can produce losses greater than the deposit; a forced sale is not a guaranteed loss cap. Rules differ by product and jurisdiction, and 10x leverage is not universally permitted. Understand the contract, maintenance requirements, costs and possible additional liability before using leverage.
groups.mid: Margin trading lets you use borrowed money or leverage to hold a larger position. With 10x leverage, $1,000 of your money can support a $10,000 position. In a simple long trade, you gain if the price rises and lose if it falls. A 10% fall would lose $1,000, using up your starting money before fees or interest. At the start, a 1% price move changes that money by about 10%. This example does not tell you when a broker will close the trade. Initial margin is what you put in to start. Maintenance margin is the equity you must keep in the account. The broker may ask for more money or sell the position before your equity reaches zero. A sudden price jump, fees and interest can make losses exceed your deposit. A forced sale does not promise to cap your loss. Rules vary by product and country. Check the terms and possible extra debt before trading.
groups.low: Margin trading means using borrowed money or leverage to hold a bigger position. With 10x leverage, $1,000 of your money supports a $10,000 trade. A long trade gains when the price rises and loses when it falls. If the price falls 10%, the loss is $1,000 before fees and interest. That uses up the starting money. At the start, a 1% price move changes your money by about 10%. This is a simple example, not a promise about when the broker will sell. Initial margin is your starting money. Maintenance margin is the equity, or your own value, that you must keep in the account. If it gets too low, the broker may demand more funds or close the trade. This can happen before your value is zero. Sudden price changes, fees and interest can leave you owing more than your deposit. A forced sale does not guarantee a limit on loss. Rules vary by product and country, so check the contract and possible extra debt first.
groups.source_review: Checked SEC margin risks and distinction between initial and maintenance margin; 10x arithmetic verified directly.
groups.notes: Corrected automatic liquidation/zero-equity assumptions and added losses beyond deposit, no universal availability.

groups.high: US market-wide circuit breakers are based on the S&P 500's percentage decline from its previous closing level. NYSE Rule 7.12 and coordinated exchange rules use 7% for Level 1, 13% for Level 2 and 20% for Level 3. A Level 1 or Level 2 trigger before 3:25 p.m. Eastern Time normally halts trading for 15 minutes, not 60 minutes. At or after 3:25 p.m., those two levels do not trigger a market-wide halt. A Level 3 decline at any time ends trading for the rest of the day. Each of the first two levels can trigger only once per trading day. These pauses allow reassessment but do not guarantee price recovery or prevent further losses. They differ from individual-security volatility pauses. SEC Regulation SHO Rule 201 concerns short-sale price restrictions following a decline in an individual stock, not the market-wide 7/13/20% system.
groups.mid: US market-wide circuit breakers pause stock trading after a large fall. They use the S&P 500 and compare it with the last day's close. NYSE Rule 7.12 uses three levels: 7%, 13% and 20%. Level 1 is a 7% fall. Level 2 is a 13% fall. Before 3:25 p.m. Eastern Time, either level normally stops trading for 15 minutes. Level 2 is not a 60-minute pause. At or after 3:25 p.m., these two levels do not cause a market-wide stop. Each can trigger only once a day. Level 3 is a 20% fall. At any time of day, it closes trading for the rest of that day. A trading suspension gives participants time to assess the news. It does not promise prices will recover or stop further loss. Rules for one stock differ. SEC Rule 201 concerns short-sale price limits after a fall in one stock. It is not the market-wide circuit-breaker rule.
groups.low: A large stock-market decline can trigger a US trading suspension. These market-wide circuit breakers use the S&P 500. They measure its fall from the last day's close. NYSE Rule 7.12 has three levels. Level 1 means a 7% fall. Level 2 means a 13% fall. Before 3:25 p.m. Eastern Time, either one normally stops trading for 15 minutes. It is not 60 minutes at Level 2. At or after 3:25 p.m., these two levels do not stop the whole market. Each can trigger just once a day. Level 3 means a 20% fall. At any time, this ends trading for the rest of the day. A trading suspension gives participants time to assess events. It does not mean prices will rise or losses will stop. A pause for just one stock has other rules. SEC Rule 201 limits some short-sale prices after one stock falls. It is not this 7%, 13%, 20% system.
groups.source_review: Checked NYSE thresholds, 15-minute halts, time-of-day and once-per-level limits.
groups.notes: Corrected 60-minute Level 2 halt, SEC Rule 201 attribution, outdated NASD authority and guaranteed recovery implications.

groups.high: If a particular fund's prospectus imposes a 2% contingent deferred sales charge on redemption within 365 days, selling within that period can reduce the proceeds. This is a fund-specific example, not a universal mutual-fund rule. A contingent deferred sales charge (CDSC) is a back-end or deferred sales load, not a front-end load. Its rate, holding-period calculation, fee base and exemptions must be checked in the prospectus. The charge may be based on the lower of original cost and current value rather than automatically on current net asset value. If a 2% charge applies to a $10,000 fee base, the charge is $200, leaving $9,800 before other costs or tax. A redemption fee differs from a sales load and may also apply under separate terms. Reaching 365 days removes the charge only if the actual schedule says so; other fees or taxes may remain. Consider liquidity needs and costs rather than assuming that waiting guarantees a better investment result.
groups.mid: Check the fund's prospectus before selling. In the example, it charges 2% if you leave within 365 days. That is a rule for that fund, not for all funds. The fee is called a contingent deferred sales charge, or CDSC. It is a back-end sales fee, paid when you sell. It is not a front-end fee paid when you buy. Check the dates, rate, amount the fee uses and any exceptions. Some funds use the lower of the purchase cost and current value. Do not assume the fee always uses today's value. If the fee base is $10,000, 2% is $200. You would have $9,800 before other costs and tax. A redemption fee is a different type of charge and may also apply. The sales fee ends at 365 days only if the fund's real terms say so. Other fees and taxes may remain. Think about when you need your money. Waiting to avoid a fee does not guarantee a better return.
groups.low: Read the fund's prospectus before you redeem your shares. This example has a 2% fee for leaving within 365 days. Not all funds have that rule. It is called a contingent deferred sales charge, or CDSC. It is a fee paid when you sell, not when you buy. Check how the fund calculates the holding period and what amount the 2% is based on. There may be exceptions. Some funds use the lower of what you paid and what the shares are worth now. Do not assume it always uses today's value. A 2% fee on $10,000 is $200. That leaves $9,800 before other costs or tax. A redemption fee is a different charge. The fund may have that too. After 365 days, this fee ends only if the real rules say so. Other fees and taxes may still apply. Think about when you need the cash. Waiting to avoid one fee does not promise a better return.
groups.source_review: Checked SEC fee definitions and prospectus dependence. No identifiable fund prospectus supplied, so 2%/365-day claim retained only as a conditional example.
groups.notes: Corrected front-end terminology and universal NAV fee-base assumption.

groups.high: In self-custody, private keys authorise transactions; a compatible recovery phrase can recreate the wallet's keys. BIP-39 specifies mnemonic phrases of 12, 15, 18, 21 or 24 words representing entropy plus a checksum. The phrase and an optional passphrase are processed into a 512-bit seed, which wallet software can use to derive keys. The phrase is not merely a website password. Anyone obtaining the necessary recovery material may be able to spend the assets. Losing the phrase does not instantly destroy funds or disable a functioning wallet: existing keys, device access or another valid backup may still permit recovery or transfer. If all usable keys and recovery material are lost, a self-custodied wallet generally has no central password-reset service. If an extra BIP-39 passphrase was used, the words alone are insufficient. Keep secure offline backups, protect them from theft and damage, and never share them with supposed support staff or enter them into an untrusted site. Custodial services have different recovery arrangements.
groups.mid: Private keys let a self-custody wallet approve a transaction. A recovery phrase can recreate those keys in a compatible wallet. BIP-39 phrases can have 12, 15, 18, 21 or 24 words. They encode random data and a check value. The words and any extra passphrase make a 512-bit seed. The wallet uses it to derive keys. This is not just a website password. A thief with the needed recovery material may spend the funds. Losing the words does not make money disappear. A working wallet, saved keys or another valid backup may still let you move it. But if all keys and recovery material are lost, there is usually no central service to reset access. If you used an extra BIP-39 passphrase, the words alone will not recover that wallet. Keep secure offline backups safe from theft and damage. Never share them with someone claiming to be support or type them into an untrusted site. A service that holds assets for you may have different recovery rules.
groups.low: A private key lets your own wallet approve a transaction. A recovery phrase can rebuild the keys in a wallet that supports it. BIP-39 phrases have 12, 15, 18, 21 or 24 words. The words hold random data and a check value. They work with any extra passphrase to make a 512-bit seed, which is used to make keys. The phrase is not just a website password. A thief with the needed words and passphrase may spend your funds. Losing the words does not destroy the money or switch off a working wallet. The device, saved keys or another backup may still let you move the funds. If you lose all keys and recovery material, there is usually no central reset service. An extra BIP-39 passphrase must be kept too; the words alone are not enough. Keep backups offline and safe from theft and damage. Never give them to supposed support staff or type them into an untrusted site. A service holding your assets may use different recovery rules.
groups.source_review: Checked BIP-39 entropy, word counts, 512-bit seed and passphrase mechanics.
groups.notes: Corrected loss-of-phrase equals immediate total-loss claim, entropy/seed confusion and assertion that ledger funds cease to exist.

groups.high: A short sale generally involves borrowing shares, selling them and later buying replacement shares to return to the lender. Profit results if the repurchase price is lower, before borrowing costs and fees. Loss results if it is higher. Unlike a fully paid long stock purchase, a short stock position has theoretically unlimited loss because the price has no fixed upper limit. The maximum gross gain is limited by a fall to zero. For example, selling 100 borrowed shares at $100 raises $10,000. Repurchasing them at $1,000 costs $100,000, a $90,000 loss before costs. That is 900% of the initial sale proceeds, not necessarily 900% of the investor's deposited capital. Maintenance-margin demands and forced close-outs can occur as losses grow. These mechanisms do not guarantee that losses remain within the margin deposit, particularly during price gaps or short squeezes. Borrowing fees and payments replacing dividends add costs. Understand these obligations before considering a short sale.
groups.mid: A short sale means selling borrowed shares and buying them back later to return them. You may gain if you buy back at a lower price, before fees and other costs. You lose if the price rises. A stock can keep rising with no fixed upper limit, so a short sale can have unlimited losses in theory. Its biggest gross gain is limited to the price falling to zero. Suppose you sell 100 borrowed shares at $100 each. You get $10,000. If you must buy them back at $1,000 each, they cost $100,000. The loss is $90,000 before costs. That is 900% of the sale proceeds, not necessarily of your own deposit. The broker may demand more funds or close the trade. This does not promise to limit your loss to the deposit. Price jumps and a short squeeze can make losses grow fast. Borrowing fees and payments for dividends also add costs. Check these duties before using short sales.
groups.low: A short sale involves selling borrowed shares and later buying replacements to return them. If you buy them back for less, you may gain after costs. If the price rises, you lose. A stock has no fixed top price. A short sale can therefore have unlimited loss in theory. The biggest gross gain is capped: the price can fall only to zero. Sell 100 shares at $100 and you get $10,000. Buy them back at $1,000 each and you pay $100,000. That is a $90,000 loss before costs. It is 900% of the sale proceeds, not always 900% of your deposit. The broker may ask for more money or close the trade. That does not cap the loss at what you put in. Sudden price jumps and a short squeeze can make the loss much worse. Borrowing fees and payments to replace dividends create additional costs too. Know the costs and duties before you short shares.
groups.source_review: Checked SEC short-sale mechanics and uncapped loss; scenario arithmetic verified.
groups.notes: Corrected claims long upside is capped and forced liquidation limits short losses to deposit. Corrected 900% denominator.

groups.high: If prices rise by a constant 7% annually and cash earns no interest, purchasing power falls to about half after 10 years. The exact doubling time for prices is ln(2)/ln(1.07), approximately 10.24 years; the Rule of 72 gives 72/7, about 10.29 years. After 10 years, prices are about 1.967 times their starting level. Cash of $10,000 still has a nominal balance of $10,000 but buys roughly $5,083 worth of the original basket, not a basket now costing $21,000. The loss compounds; it is not a simple 70% subtraction. Exact annual real return equals (1 + nominal return)/(1 + inflation) minus 1. At zero interest and 7% inflation, that is about −6.54%, not exactly −7%. With 3% interest it is about −3.74%. Matching inflation preserves purchasing power before tax and costs. Investments can lose value, so inflation does not justify treating any asset as a guaranteed hedge; retain appropriate emergency liquidity and consider risk and time horizon.
groups.mid: If prices rise 7% each year and cash earns no interest, its buying power falls to about half in 10 years. The balance does not fall, but prices rise. The exact doubling time is ln(2)/ln(1.07), about 10.24 years. The Rule of 72 estimates it as 72 divided by 7, or about 10.29 years. After 10 years, prices are about 1.967 times as high. Your $10,000 still says $10,000, but buys about $5,083 worth of today's goods. Those goods would now cost about $19,672, not $21,000. The loss builds on itself; it is not 7% times 10. Real return means your inflation-adjusted investment return. The exact yearly calculation divides 1 plus the interest rate by 1 plus inflation, then subtracts 1. At 0% interest, that is about −6.54%; at 3% interest, about −3.74%. Matching inflation preserves buying power before tax and costs. No investment is a guaranteed shield. Keep cash for urgent needs and weigh risk and time before investing.
groups.low: Prices rising 7% a year can cut cash buying power in half in about 10 years. This assumes no interest. You still have the same cash balance, but it buys less. The exact doubling time is ln(2)/ln(1.07). That gives about 10.24 years. The Rule of 72 gives a rough check: 72 divided by 7 is about 10.29 years. After 10 years, prices are about 1.967 times as high. Your $10,000 buys about $5,083 worth of today's goods. A basket worth $10,000 today would cost about $19,672 then, not $21,000. This compounded loss is not a simple 70% subtraction. Real return means what you earn after inflation, the rise in prices. For the exact rate, divide 1 plus interest by 1 plus inflation, then subtract 1. At 0% interest, the rate is about −6.54%. At 3% interest, it is about −3.74%. Matching inflation keeps buying power before tax and costs. No investment promises to beat inflation. Keep cash for urgent needs and check risk and time before investing.
groups.source_review: Checked real-return framework; compound growth figures calculated directly.
groups.notes: Corrected 10-year basket price, exact real returns and guaranteed inflation-hedge implications.

groups.high: US-source dividends paid to a nonresident alien individual are generally subject to 30% withholding on the gross amount when not effectively connected with a US trade or business. An applicable income-tax treaty may reduce the rate, subject to residence, beneficial-ownership and other eligibility conditions. It is not automatically reduced because someone lives abroad. Provide a properly completed Form W-8BEN to the withholding agent to establish foreign status and claim eligible treaty benefits; entities generally use different forms, such as W-8BEN-E. The agent ordinarily reports the payment and withholding on Form 1042-S. A $100 gross dividend leaves $70 at a 30% rate before other charges. Effectively connected income follows different rules. Filing Form 1040-NR is not universally required solely because a fully withheld dividend was received; filing obligations depend on the facts. A return may be needed to claim a refund of excess withholding or pay additional tax. Check the actual treaty, IRS guidance and any home-country reporting or relief rather than assuming US withholding settles every tax obligation.
groups.mid: A nonresident alien individual usually faces 30% withholding on US-source dividends. The tax applies to the gross amount. This generally applies when the income is not effectively connected with a US trade or business. At 30%, a $100 dividend leaves $70 before other charges. An income-tax treaty may reduce the rate. You must meet its residence, beneficial ownership and other conditions. Living abroad alone does not establish eligibility. Give Form W-8BEN to the withholding agent, usually the broker or payer. It confirms foreign status and claims treaty benefits if you are eligible. Companies and other entities normally use different forms, such as W-8BEN-E. The payer usually reports the dividend and tax on Form 1042-S. Income linked to a US business can follow different rules. Receiving a fully withheld dividend does not automatically require every person to file Form 1040-NR. Filing depends on the facts. It may be needed to recover excess withholding or pay extra tax. Check the treaty, IRS rules and home-country tax duties. US withholding does not settle all possible taxes.
groups.low: US-source dividends paid to a nonresident alien usually have 30% tax taken from the full amount. This applies in general when the income is not effectively connected with a US business. A $100 dividend then leaves $70 before other charges. A tax treaty may allow a lower rate. You must meet its rules on residence, ownership and other conditions. Living abroad is not enough by itself. Give Form W-8BEN to the broker or other payer to show foreign status and claim treaty benefits if eligible. It is for individuals. A company may need W-8BEN-E or another form. The payer normally reports the dividend and tax on Form 1042-S. Income connected to a US business has different rules. A fully withheld dividend does not mean everyone must file Form 1040-NR. Filing depends on the case. You may need a return to claim back excess tax or pay more that is due. Check IRS guidance, the treaty and your home-country rules. US withholding may not cover every tax duty.
groups.source_review: Checked IRS non-ECI dividend withholding, treaty claims and return qualifications.
groups.notes: Corrected effectively-connected-income treatment, W-8BEN description and blanket return-filing claim.

groups.high: Credit utilisation is the proportion of available revolving credit represented by reported balances. A $900 reported balance on a $3,000 limit gives 30% utilisation. FICO considers both overall usage and individual accounts as part of its assessment of amounts owed. That broader category accounts for roughly 30% of a typical FICO score; utilisation alone is not necessarily 30% of the score. Higher usage can lower scores, but 30% is not a universal cliff where damage suddenly begins. Generally, lower reported usage is preferable, although effects vary by scoring model and credit profile. Pay on time and avoid unnecessary debt; carrying interest-bearing balances is not required to build a score. Check when issuers report balances, since the reported amount may differ from the current balance. Paying down a balance can reduce utilisation. A higher limit may also reduce the ratio, but a request can have costs, inquiry effects or encourage overspending. Do not treat a percentage target as a guarantee of a particular score.
groups.mid: Credit utilisation means how much of your available revolving credit you use. A $900 balance on a $3,000 card limit is 30%. FICO looks at total usage and each account. This is part of amounts owed, a wider category worth roughly 30% of a typical FICO score. It does not mean utilisation alone always makes up 30%. High usage can hurt your score, but 30% is not a fixed cliff where all harm starts. Lower reported usage is generally better. Results vary by score model and your credit record. Pay on time and avoid debt you do not need. You do not have to carry a balance and pay interest to build a score. Check when the card company reports your balance. That amount may differ from what you owe today. Paying it down can lower usage. A higher limit can lower the ratio too, but asking for one may affect your credit or lead to more spending. No percentage promises a fixed score.
groups.low: Credit utilisation is the share of a credit limit you use. A $900 balance on a $3,000 limit is 30%. FICO checks the total and each account. Usage is part of the amounts-owed category. That whole category is about 30% of a typical score, not usage alone. High usage can hurt a score. But 30% is not a magic line where all harm starts. Lower reported use is usually better. The effect depends on the score model and your record. Pay on time. Do not take on debt you do not need. You do not need to pay interest on a carried balance to build credit. Check when the card company reports the balance. That may not be the same as today's balance. Paying debt down can lower the ratio. A bigger limit can too. But asking for one may affect your credit or tempt more spending. No set percentage guarantees a score.
groups.source_review: Checked FICO's explicit rejection of 30% universal threshold and amounts-owed distinction.
groups.notes: Corrected fabricated cliff, stable-30-to-50 claim and score-maximisation guarantees.

groups.high: A guaranteed 20% monthly investment return is an extreme fraud warning, especially when paired with claims of little or no risk. It is not sufficient evidence by itself to diagnose the legal structure of a Ponzi scheme, and high returns are not mathematically impossible. At 20% monthly compounding, $1,000 would become about $8,916 after 12 months, a gain of about 792%; that illustrates the extraordinary promise, not a realistic forecast. A Ponzi scheme pays supposed returns to existing investors using new investors' money instead of genuine investment earnings. It depends on continuing inflows and may collapse when recruitment slows or withdrawals rise. Warning signs include secrecy, unregistered sellers, missing documentation and difficulty withdrawing funds. Do not send money because of a guarantee, pressure or early successful payouts. Verify the seller and investment independently through the relevant regulator, retain records and report suspected fraud. Registration is not a guarantee of investment safety. Avoid claiming that every participant must lose 100%; the appropriate conclusion is severe risk of loss and fraud.
groups.mid: A promise of guaranteed 20% returns each month is a serious fraud warning. Be especially wary if the seller says there is little or no risk. The number is not mathematically impossible, but it is an extraordinary promise, not a safe forecast. If $1,000 grew by 20% each month, it would become about $8,916 after a year. That is a gain of about 792%. A Ponzi scheme pays older investors with money from new investors rather than real investment earnings. It needs new cash to keep going and may collapse when people stop joining or ask to withdraw. The promise alone does not prove the exact type of fraud. Look for secrecy, missing records, unregistered sellers and blocked withdrawals. Do not send money just because someone guarantees a return or shows an early payout. Check the seller and product independently with the relevant regulator. Registration does not guarantee safety. Keep records and report suspected fraud. The risk is severe; it is not accurate to say every person must lose 100%.
groups.low: A guaranteed 20% return each month is a big warning sign. Be wary of claims of no risk. The maths is possible, but that does not make the promise safe or likely. At 20% a month, $1,000 would grow to about $8,916 in a year. That is about 792% profit. It shows how large the promise is, not what you should expect. In a Ponzi scheme, new people's money pays old investors. It is not paid from real earnings. The scheme may fail when new cash stops or people want their money back. The return alone does not prove that this is the exact type of fraud. Watch for secrets, missing papers, unregistered sellers or trouble taking cash out. Do not pay because of pressure, a guarantee or one early payout. Check the seller and product with the right regulator yourself. Being registered does not prove safety. Keep records and report suspected fraud. You could lose a lot. It is not true that every person must lose all their money.
groups.source_review: Checked SEC Ponzi definition/red flags; compound arithmetic verified.
groups.notes: Corrected false compounding sequence, mathematical-impossibility claim and certainty of 100% losses/Ponzi diagnosis.

groups.high: Asset allocation divides a portfolio among categories such as equities, bonds and cash according to risk tolerance, goals and time horizon. Different returns cause the proportions to drift, changing the portfolio's risk. Rebalancing restores the intended mix through sales and purchases or by directing new contributions towards underweight assets. A 5-percentage-point tolerance band is one optional policy, not a universal investment rule. For a 60% equity target, a band of 5 percentage points means reviewing a move above 65% or below 55%; a 5% relative deviation would produce different thresholds. Specify which interpretation the plan uses and whether action is triggered at or beyond the boundary. Consider fees, taxes, liquidity and account restrictions before trading. A scheduled review is another possible approach. Rebalancing can support disciplined risk control but does not guarantee profits, prevent losses or prove that selling recent winners is always beneficial. Review the underlying target when personal circumstances change rather than mechanically preserving an unsuitable allocation.
groups.mid: Asset allocation is how you split investments among shares, bonds, cash and other types. Choose a mix that fits your goals, time and risk tolerance. Different investment returns cause the proportions of the portfolio to drift. This may make the plan riskier or more cautious than you want. Rebalancing means restoring the intended mix. You can buy and sell, or put new money into the parts that are too small. A 5-percentage-point band is one choice, not a rule for everyone. If shares should be 60%, such a band runs from 55% to 65%. A 5% relative change gives different limits. Say which rule you mean and whether the trigger is at or beyond the limit. Check fees, tax and how easily you can trade. Reviews on set dates are another option. Rebalancing helps manage risk; it does not promise gains or stop loss. If your needs change, review the target too rather than keeping an unsuitable plan.
groups.low: Asset allocation means splitting your money among investments such as shares, bonds and cash. The mix should fit your goals, time and risk tolerance. Prices move, so one part can become too large or small. Your risk may change. Rebalancing brings the mix back to its target. You can sell overweight investments, buy underweight investments or direct new contributions to the smaller parts. A 5-percentage-point band is one optional rule. It is not a rule for everyone. A 60% target for shares would have limits of 55% and 65%. A 5% relative change means something else and gives different limits. State which rule you use and whether action starts at or beyond the limit. Check tax, fees and limits on selling before trading. You can also review the mix on set dates. Rebalancing helps control risk, but it cannot guarantee profit or stop all loss. When your needs change, review the target too. Do not keep a plan that no longer fits.
groups.source_review: Checked SEC allocation and rebalancing guidance; numerical band is explicit example, not mandated rule.
groups.notes: Corrected absolute five-percent mandate, percentage/percentage-point ambiguity and guaranteed buy-low/sell-high benefits.
